processing: For home use, mature leaves are washed, scrubbed of the fuzz on their undersides, baked until crisp and crushed. Commercial products vary and may be roasted.
harvest_season: Leaves of an evergreen tree, not tied to a prized picking; older, mature leaves are preferred, ideally two years or more.
appearance_dry: Crushed brown-green to dark brown pieces of tough leaf.
appearance_liquor: Clear red-brown, deeper in roasted versions.
taste_profile: Mild and easy, close to a soft oolong or roasted tea, with a little earth and little aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Best simmered: a common home ratio is 20 g of crushed leaf to 1 litre of water for about 20 minutes on low heat. Remove the fuzz from fresh leaves first.

vintage_note: Sold with no vintage, as loose leaf or tea bags, all year. Roasted and unroasted versions taste different, so check which you are getting.
description:
Biwa-cha is an infusion of loquat leaves, from the same tree that gives the small orange fruit. It is a Japanese home preparation that is also sold packaged, with no true tea in it.

Home makers want older leaves, scrub the fuzz off the underside, bake them until crisp and crush them. Baking and any further roasting are what give the cup its brown colour.

The result is a gentle cup somewhere near oolong or hojicha, with little to dislike. Because the leaf is tough it wants a long simmer rather than a short steep. Some people add milk, and it takes to that well.

Ignore the bigger promises on the box, since effects in people are not established. Look for origin on the label and buy for an easy evening drink.
history: Little is documented about the history of this tea. Loquat leaves are generally described as a Japanese home remedy, and the date of the first cup remains unknown.
